To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we provide the first algorithm that achieves a sub-linear regret in a piecewise-stochastic bandit problem with adversarial changes, and that we do so by leveraging a small number of side observations.

(i) side observations on past actions can significantly improve performance in adversarial bandit problems; (ii) in piecewise-stationarity bandit problems with unknown change points, a limited number of observations on past rewards is enough to achieve the optimal regret; (iii) the algorithm can be implemented in a distributed fashion.
(a) side observations are helpful in the context of piecewise-stationarity and (b) the benefit of side observations can be significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How can we use side information to improve the performance of an algorithm in the bandit framework?
the following problem: A player is playing against an adversary who is choosing the reward distributions at each time step.
the following question: how can we learn to play optimally when the environment is adversarial?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of side observations can reduce the regret from Ω(√T) to O(k log(T)) in a piecewise-stationsry bandit problem with an adversarial reward process.
our approach is a first attempt towards the development of a theory for piecewise-stationarity in bandit problems with limited side information.
the use of side observations allows to reduce the regret from the worst-case Ω(√T) to the best-case O(k log(T)).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the side observations allow us to recover the performance of a non-adaptive policy, even in a worst-case scenario.
we provide a regret bound that depends on the number of distribution changes, rather than on the time T.
, when side observations are available, the problem can be reduced to the case where the reward distribution is stationary, and the algorithm can be applied as is.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of side observations, it is possible to learn the optimal policy without knowing the number of changes.
side observations can be used to obtain a regret bound that depends only on the number of changes, and not on their frequency.
side information can significantly improve the performance of algorithms in the adversarial setting, and that this improvement can be obtained even when the side information is noisy.
